title: Jeremiah 36:9–19
context: The narrator moves to the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month, when a fast is proclaimed in Jerusalem (36:9). Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words in the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan, in the hearing of all the people (36:10). Gemariah’s son Micaiah reports the words to the princes gathered in the scribe’s room, and they send Jehudi to bring Baruch with the scroll (36:11–14). The princes hear it, turn to one another in fear, and resolve to tell the king (36:15–16). They ask how the words were written, and Baruch answers that Jeremiah dictated them and he wrote them with ink (36:17–18). The princes then tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (36:19). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the word of God is taken seriously by some hearers, and the princes’ fear and their care for the prophet and the scribe stand in contrast to the king’s response in the next unit.

verses.text: Now in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem, proclaimed a fast before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: In the fifth year, in the ninth month, the people proclaimed a fast before the LORD. Arminian readers note the setting: a public occasion of seeking God, which gave an opportunity to hear his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the fast as the occasion for the reading. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical setting, and neither speculates about the reasons for the fast beyond what the text says.

verses.text: Then Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the book in the LORD’s house, in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the upper court, at the entry of the new gate of the LORD’s house, in the ears of all the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Baruch read in the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan, “in the ears of all the people.” Arminian readers note the public reading. The word is placed before everyone gathered at the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word proclaimed openly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the word was made available to all, and both note the role of Shaphan’s family in the narrative (compare 26:24).

verses.text: When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the LORD’s words,
verses.arminianNotes: Micaiah son of Gemariah heard “all the LORD’s words.” Arminian readers note that one hearer takes the words seriously enough to report them. The word begins to move beyond the crowd.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word reaching a hearer who acts on it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing how the word spreads through those who hear and respond, setting up the scene with the princes.

verses.text: he went down into the king’s house, into the scribe’s room; and behold, all the princes were sitting there, Elishama the scribe, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
verses.arminianNotes: Micaiah goes to the scribe’s room, where all the princes are sitting. Arminian readers note the list of officials. The word now reaches those with power in the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word moving toward the royal court. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as narrative detail, and neither builds conclusions on the names beyond what the text provides.

verses.text: Then Micaiah declared to them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Micaiah declares all the words he had heard. Arminian readers note that the message is passed on faithfully. The princes hear what Baruch read to the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the faithful report of what was heard. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the word continuing to spread, and as preparing for the princes’ request to hear it directly.

verses.text: Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, to Baruch, saying, “Take in your hand the scroll in which you have read in the ears of the people, and come.” So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand, and came to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes send Jehudi to bring Baruch and the scroll. Arminian readers note the officials’ interest. They want to hear the words for themselves, not only a report of them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the princes taking the word seriously. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a willingness to hear, and both note Baruch’s readiness to come with the scroll.

verses.text: They said to him, “Sit down now, and read it in our hearing.” So Baruch read it in their hearing.
verses.arminianNotes: “Sit down now, and read it in our hearing.” Arminian readers note the courteous reception. The princes receive Baruch respectfully and listen to the reading.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a respectful hearing of the word. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as contrasting the princes’ attentiveness with the king’s later response.

verses.text: Now when they had heard all the words, they turned in fear one toward another, and said to Baruch, “We will surely tell the king of all these words.”
verses.arminianNotes: They “turned in fear one toward another” and resolved to tell the king. Arminian readers note the right response of fear at God’s word. The princes recognize the seriousness of what they have heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see fear as a fitting response to the word of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the princes’ awe, which stands in contrast to the king and his servants, who “were not afraid” (36:24).

verses.text: They asked Baruch, saying, “Tell us now, how did you write all these words at his mouth?”
verses.arminianNotes: They ask Baruch how he wrote the words “at his mouth.” Arminian readers note the princes’ concern for the source. They want to know whether these are truly Jeremiah’s words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a question about how the word was received and written. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the princes’ careful inquiry, and neither builds a theory of inspiration on it.

verses.text: Then Baruch answered them, “He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.”
verses.arminianNotes: “He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.” Arminian readers note Baruch’s simple answer. He was the scribe; the words came from Jeremiah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a plain description of the prophet’s dictation and the scribe’s writing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as reporting Baruch’s role as the text states, without expanding it into a broader theory.

verses.text: Then the princes said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah go hide. Don’t let anyone know where you are.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You and Jeremiah go hide.” Arminian readers note the princes’ concern for the safety of the prophet and scribe. They expect the king to react with hostility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the princes acting to protect God’s messengers. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an act of care for Baruch and Jeremiah, preparing for the danger of the next unit.
